title: Are Some Students Smarter Than Others?
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Prompted by a moment when an administrator wrote off a struggling student as simply 'not very smart,' Dylan Kane surveys intelligence research and translates it into classroom-actionable terms. He explains general intelligence (g), the split between crystallized intelligence (accumulated knowledge) and fluid intelligence (processing speed and working memory), and the Flynn effect showing intelligence has risen across generations as evidence that 'smart' is not a fixed, unchangeable label. His central argument is that thinking in terms of crystallized intelligence, processing speed, and working memory is more useful and less fatalistic than the blanket label 'smart,' because each of those components points to something a teacher can actually act on: teach more content, scaffold for processing speed, reduce working memory load. He argues systematic, structured teaching narrows the learning-speed gap between students who pick things up quickly and those who need more support, using phonics as his central example, and that crystallized intelligence matters more than fluid intelligence in practice because knowledge in long-term memory reduces the burden on working memory and processing speed for everything downstream. He closes with a practical roadmap: scaffold, teach specific content, break concepts into systematically taught pieces, fill prior-knowledge gaps, avoid labels, and refuse to give up on students who seem stuck.
points: Kane reframes 'smart' into three actionable components, crystallized intelligence, processing speed, and working memory, arguing each points to a concrete teacher intervention unlike the fatalistic blanket label.
He argues systematic, small-steps teaching (using phonics as the paradigm case) narrows the achievement gap between students who learn quickly unaided and those who need more structure.

He argues crystallized intelligence matters more than fluid intelligence in practice, because knowledge already in long-term memory reduces the working-memory and processing-speed burden of everything a student does afterward.

He closes with an explicit six-item action list (scaffold, teach specific content, break concepts down, fill prior-knowledge gaps, avoid labels, don't give up) meant to replace vague 'high expectations' rhetoric with concrete practice.
quotes: That sentence hung in the air. The implication was clear: maybe we should give up. The student wasn't in special education.

Does intelligence matter? In short, yes. Scoring higher on tests like IQ is correlated with lots of positive things, like lifetime earnings, educational attainment, lack of involvement with the criminal justice system, and more.
Crystallized intelligence is the name for all of the knowledge, skills, and experiences that help us to navigate the world.
It’s helpful for teachers to think in terms of crystallized intelligence, processing speed, and working memory, rather than “smart.

A number of studies suggest that when teachers break skills down into small, manageable parts, teach those parts one at a time, and systematically build up to bigger and bigger ideas, differences in learning speed are narrower.
Knowledge in long-term memory, crystallized intelligence, reduces demands on working memory and processing speed. We think faster when we draw on stuff we know.
Too many students feel dumb in school. They feel like the learning moves too fast, they never seem to get it before the class moves on, and they’re struggling to stay afloat.
